title: The snake sheds its skin
hookLine: the first poem: letting go as a snake leaves its worn-out skin

cards: Sometimes, on a hiking trail or under a porch, you find one: a snake's skin, papery, see-through, the whole length of the animal, even the scales over the eyes, turned inside out like a sock pulled off in one go.
The snake is nowhere near. It rubbed its nose on a rough stone, loosened the edge, and crawled forward out of the old self it had outgrown. It didn't tear anything.
It just left. The first poem of the Sutta Nipata takes that picture and repeats it, verse after verse, seventeen times.

teach.h: URAGA: THE ONE WHO MOVES ON ITS CHEST
teach.b: The poem is the Uraga Sutta. Uraga is a poetic word for snake, the one who moves on its chest.
Every verse ends with the same refrain, which runs roughly: such a monk leaves behind this shore and the far shore, as a snake leaves its worn-out old skin.
And every verse begins with a different thing let go, each with its own picture.
The first: whoever holds back anger as it rises, the way a healer stops snake venom spreading with medicine. Another: whoever cuts off desire completely, like pulling up a lotus that grew in a pond.
Another: whoever has broken down pride, the way a great flood sweeps away a flimsy bridge of reeds.

And one of the strangest: whoever finds no solid core in any kind of existence, like someone searching fig trees for flowers. Those fig trees don't show their flowers; they're hidden inside the fruit. You'll look forever.

teach.h: THE SKIN IS ALREADY WORN OUT
teach.b: Notice what the poem keeps saying about the old skin: it's worn out, already outgrown. Letting go here isn't a heroic tearing. It's leaving what no longer fits.
Then the puzzle in the refrain: this shore and the far shore. Elsewhere, the far shore is the goal. Why leave that too?

The old commentary offers several readings, one of them simply this world and the next. Some modern readers hear more: the one who's free doesn't cling even to having arrived. The poem doesn't explain itself.

how: The Uraga Sutta opens the Sutta Nipata and is studied and chanted in Theravada communities, and Buddhist teachers use its snake-and-skin image when they speak about letting go of anger and pride.

o: a lotus that grows in a muddy pond
a dragon that guards hidden treasure
a snake, the one that moves on its chest

games.q: the snake poem: tap the pairs.
p: like pulling up a lotus in a pond
like a flood sweeping away a reed bridge
like looking for flowers on a fig tree

s: the snake poem uses the same refrain in every verse
each verse ends with leaving this shore and the far shore, like a snake its worn-out skin.
in the poem, the snake tears off its skin by force
the skin is worn out and old; the snake simply leaves what it has outgrown.
the refrain is easy and everyone agrees what it means
the commentary gives several readings of this shore and the far shore.

games.q: you've found a fig tree and you're looking for its flowers, the way the poem describes. what happens?
o: you find them at the top.
you search and find none showing.
games.why: the poem uses the hidden fig flower as its picture of finding no solid core in any existence: you won't find it however long you look.

practice: Ask quietly: what am I still carrying that I've already outgrown? An old grudge, a story about yourself from ten years ago, a habit that made sense once.

Don't fight it; just see that it's worn thin, like papery skin, and on the out-breath picture slipping forward out of it and leaving it on the path, knowing you can come back for it if you really need to.

wordCard.voice: uraga. The refrain of the Sutta Nipata's first poem: letting go of anger, desire and pride the way a snake leaves a skin it has already outgrown. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali uraga: snake, literally one who moves on its chest. the name of Sn 1.1.

carryVoice: Your line: shed the old skin. Worn out, already outgrown, left on the path. That's day five hundred seventy-seven.
